articles.title: Networking Essentials for Software Engineers – Part 3: What Happens When You Type a Website Name?
articles.excerpt: Imagine we open our browser and type google.com. We want to visit Google's website. But how does our browser know which server to contact? Computers use IP addresses to communicate across networks. So…
articles.body: Imagine we open our browser and type google.com . We want to visit Google's website. But how does our browser know which server to contact? Computers use IP addresses to communicate across networks. So, our browser needs to find an IP address associated with google.com before it can connect to the website. We could use IP addresses directly, but imagine having to remember the IP addresses of Google, YouTube, Amazon, and every other website we visit. And those IP addresses might change over time. Remembering website names is much easier than remembering a bunch of numbers, right? That's why we have DNS (Domain Name System) . DNS helps us find the IP addresses associated with domain names such as google.com . But how does DNS know which IP address belongs to a particular domain?

articles.title: Shrinking screenshots for a form that only takes JPG under 200 KB
articles.excerpt: Every few weeks someone on a team hits the same wall: a portal, job application or government form says "JPG only, max 200 KB", and the file you have is a 2.4 MB PNG screenshot or a WebP you saved fro…
articles.body: Every few weeks someone on a team hits the same wall: a portal, job application or government form says "JPG only, max 200 KB", and the file you have is a 2.4 MB PNG screenshot or a WebP you saved from a browser. A few things worth knowing before you start fiddling: 1. Format first, then size. PNG is lossless, so screenshots with lots of text stay big. Converting to JPG alone often cuts the file by 70–90%. WebP is even smaller, but many older upload forms still reject it, which is why "JPG only" keeps showing up. 2. Resize before you crank down quality. A 3000 px wide screenshot shown in a 600 px box wastes most of its bytes. Dropping the width to around 1200–1600 px usually gets you under the limit while text stays readable.

articles.title: The light we built
articles.excerpt: In 2017 I built a room you could not read. It was a cube, a timber frame wrapped in fabric, and on the fabric I had painted quotes about life, death and perception. You could walk in and stand surroun…
articles.body: In 2017 I built a room you could not read. It was a cube, a timber frame wrapped in fabric, and on the fabric I had painted quotes about life, death and perception. You could walk in and stand surrounded by them and see nothing. The paint was ultraviolet. In visible light the walls were blank. Only when the light shifted beyond what the eye can see did the words appear, glowing, all at once, as if they had been there the whole time. They had. The line at the centre of it was from The Little Prince : "What is essential is invisible to the eye." That was my MA. A Journey Through Light. Three volumes, a cube, six GoPros filming in every direction so it could be walked through again as a virtual space.
articles.author: Sammii

articles.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
articles.excerpt: For over a century astronomers have speculated that comets could have delivered organic molecules necessary for life to Earth, but new modeling shows these molecules wouldn't have survived impact.
articles.body: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

articles.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
articles.excerpt: This dazzling collection of ancient stars could hold clues to the Milky Way's past.
articles.body: The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus.

articles.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
articles.excerpt: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.
articles.body: A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.
